title: How Government Works
tagline: Who makes decisions, and who to go to for what.
description: Government can feel far away, but it decides things that touch your life every day: roads, clinics, schools, water and markets. This course explains, in plain language, how Zambia's government is organised, from State House to your ward, so you know who is responsible for what and how to reach them.
outcomes: Name the three arms of government and what each does
Explain the roles of the President, Parliament and the courts
Describe how provinces, districts and councils work
Know the role of your MP, councillor and ward development committee
Know your main rights and responsibilities as a citizen
Choose the right office for a common problem

modules.title: The three arms of government
modules.summary: The executive, Parliament and the courts.

lessons.title: Who makes the rules
lessons.body:
Zambia is a democracy. Power belongs to the people, who choose leaders in elections. The **Constitution** is the highest law. It sets out how government is organised and the rights of every person.

To stop any one person or group from having too much power, government is divided into **three arms**. Each one checks the others.

## 1. The Legislature (Parliament)
The **National Assembly** makes laws, approves the national budget, and questions the government on its work. Its members are mainly **Members of Parliament (MPs)**, each elected by the people of one **constituency**.

## 2. The Executive
The **President**, the **Vice-President** and **Cabinet ministers** run the country day to day. Ministries, like Health or Education, and the civil servants who work in them, put laws and policies into action.

## 3. The Judiciary (the courts)
The courts settle disputes and decide whether laws have been broken. They also decide whether actions by government follow the Constitution. Judges must be **independent**, meaning nobody can tell them how to decide a case.

## Why three arms?
Think of a three-legged stool. If one leg is too long or too short, the stool falls. Parliament can question the executive. The courts can stop unlawful actions. The executive carries out the work. Together they keep power balanced.

## Where you fit
You choose the President, your MP, your mayor or council chairperson, and your councillor in **general elections**, held every five years.
key_points: The Constitution is the highest law
Three arms: Parliament, the executive and the courts
Each arm checks the others

lessons.title: The President, ministers and ministries
lessons.body:
The **executive** is the part of government that does the work of running the country.

## The President
The President is the **Head of State** and **Head of Government**, elected directly by voters. The President leads the Cabinet, appoints ministers and many senior officials, and is Commander-in-Chief of the Defence Force. A President can serve a maximum of two terms.

## The Vice-President
The Vice-President is elected together with the President as a running mate, and takes over if the President cannot continue.

## Cabinet ministers
The President appoints **ministers** to lead ministries, such as Health, Education, Agriculture, and Local Government. Together they form the **Cabinet**, which makes key government decisions.

## Ministries and civil servants
Each **ministry** has offices at national, provincial and district level, staffed by **civil servants**: teachers, nurses, agricultural officers, social welfare officers and many more. They stay in their jobs when governments change, so services continue.

## Other public bodies
Many services are run by **public bodies** set up by law, such as ZESCO for electricity, water utilities, the Zambia Revenue Authority, and regulators like ZICTA. They report to a ministry.

## Why it matters to you
When a clinic has no medicine or a school has no teacher, the problem usually sits with a **ministry's district office**. Knowing that helps you take the problem to the right place.
key_points: The President leads the executive and is elected directly
Ministers lead ministries; civil servants deliver services
Many problems are handled by a ministry's district office
lessons.try_it: Name one ministry and one service it provides in your area.

lessons.title: Parliament and the courts
lessons.body:
## The National Assembly
Parliament sits in Lusaka. Its main jobs are to:

- **Make laws.** A proposed law is called a **Bill**. MPs debate it, and once passed and signed by the President, it becomes an **Act**.
- **Approve the budget**, deciding how public money is spent.
- **Oversee the government.** MPs ask ministers questions, and **committees** examine how ministries spend money and do their work.
- **Represent you.** Your MP should bring your constituency's concerns to Parliament.

Most MPs are elected by constituencies. A small number are nominated by the President. The **Speaker** chairs the sittings. Many sittings are broadcast on radio and TV, and the National Assembly website publishes debates and reports.

## The courts
Zambia's courts include:

- **Local Courts**, which handle many customary matters such as some marriage and family disputes.
- **Subordinate Courts** (magistrates), which hear most criminal and civil cases.
- The **High Court**, for more serious cases and appeals.
- The **Court of Appeal**.
- The **Supreme Court** and the **Constitutional Court**, the highest courts. The Constitutional Court decides questions about the Constitution.

## Traditional leaders
**Chiefs** play an important role in their chiefdoms, especially over customary land and culture. The **House of Chiefs** advises government on traditional matters. Chiefs are expected to stay out of party politics.
key_points: Parliament makes laws, approves the budget and checks government
A Bill becomes an Act when passed and signed
Courts range from Local Courts to the Supreme and Constitutional Courts

lessons.title: Provinces, districts and councils
lessons.body:
Zambia is divided into **10 provinces** and **116 districts**. This lets services be planned and delivered closer to people.

## Provinces
Each province has a **Provincial Minister** and a **Permanent Secretary**, who coordinate government work in the province.

## Districts and councils
Each district has a **local authority**, usually called a **council**. Depending on size, it is a **city council**, a **municipal council** or a **town council**.

Councils are led by an elected **mayor** (in cities and municipalities) or **council chairperson**, and made up of elected **councillors**, one for each **ward**. A **town clerk** or **council secretary** heads the council staff.

## What councils do
Councils are responsible for many things you see every day, such as:

- markets and bus stations,
- local roads and drainage,
- refuse collection,
- business levies and some licences,
- planning and building permits,
- some water and sanitation work,
- community development and social welfare in partnership with ministries.

Councils raise some money through levies, fees and property rates, and receive money from national government, such as the **Local Government Equalisation Fund** and the **Constituency Development Fund (CDF)**.

## Decentralisation
Zambia's policy of **decentralisation** aims to move more decisions and money from Lusaka to councils, so communities have more say. You can see this in CDF, where local committees decide on local projects.
key_points: 10 provinces and 116 districts
Each district has a council with elected councillors
Councils run markets, local roads, refuse and more

lessons.title: Your MP and your councillor
lessons.body:
You have elected representatives at different levels. Knowing who they are, and what they can do, helps you get problems solved.

## Your Member of Parliament (MP)
Your MP represents your **constituency** in the National Assembly. Your MP can:

- raise your constituency's problems in Parliament and with ministers,
- sit on the **CDF committee** that decides on local projects,
- help connect you with the right ministry.

Most MPs have a **constituency office**. You can visit, write or call.

## Your ward councillor
Your **councillor** represents your **ward** on the district council. Councillors are often the easiest elected leader to reach. They can:

- raise ward issues in council meetings,
- follow up on council services such as markets, roads and refuse,
- work with your **Ward Development Committee**.

## Your mayor or council chairperson
They lead the council and its meetings.

## Ward Development Committees (WDCs)
The **Local Government Act of 2019** provides for **Ward Development Committees**. They bring together community members to identify local needs, plan projects and monitor them. WDCs play a role in proposing CDF projects. Ask your councillor how to attend or join.

## Holding them to account
Representatives work for you. It is reasonable to ask them what they have done, what is planned, and when. Be polite, be specific, and follow up.
key_points: Your MP represents your constituency in Parliament
Your councillor represents your ward on the council
Ward Development Committees help plan local projects

lessons.title: Elections and voting
lessons.body:
Elections are how citizens choose their leaders and hold them accountable.

## General elections
Zambia holds **general elections every five years**. On the same day, voters elect:

- the **President** (with the Vice-President as running mate),
- their **Member of Parliament**,
- their **mayor or council chairperson**,
- their **ward councillor**.

There can also be **by-elections** when a seat becomes empty.

## Who can vote
Zambian citizens aged **18 or older** who are **registered** as voters. To register, you need your **NRC**. Registration happens during periods announced by the **Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ)**.

## The ECZ
The **Electoral Commission of Zambia** runs elections. It registers voters, sets polling stations, counts votes and announces results. Its official website and social media pages are the place to check dates, rules and your polling station.

## Your vote is secret
Nobody can see who you voted for. Do not let anyone pressure you, pay you or threaten you to vote a certain way, and do not take photos of your ballot.

## Beyond voting
Democracy does not stop on election day. You can attend council meetings, contact your MP, take part in your Ward Development Committee, and make your views heard peacefully.

## Be careful with election rumours
False messages about dates, places and results spread fast at election time. Check with the ECZ before you believe or share them.
key_points: General elections are every five years
Register with your NRC when the ECZ opens registration
Your vote is secret; check election facts with the ECZ
lessons.try_it: Check the ECZ's official page for information on voter registration.

modules.title: You and the government
modules.summary: Rights, responsibilities and who to go to for what.

lessons.title: Your rights and responsibilities
lessons.body:
The **Bill of Rights** in the Constitution protects the rights of every person in Zambia.

## Some of your rights
- **Life, liberty and security** of the person.
- **Equality**: protection from discrimination because of your sex, tribe, religion, disability, political opinion and more.
- **Freedom of expression**, including the right to receive and share information.
- **Freedom of assembly and association**: to meet peacefully and join groups, including political parties and unions.
- **Freedom of conscience and religion.**
- **Privacy** of your home and property.
- **Protection from torture** and inhuman treatment.
- A **fair trial** if you are accused of a crime.

Rights have limits, for example to protect other people's rights and public safety.

## Your responsibilities
Rights work when everyone also does their part:

- **Obey the law** and respect other people's rights.
- **Pay taxes**, levies and fees that fund public services.
- **Vote** and take part in community life.
- **Protect public property**, like schools, boreholes and roads.
- **Report crime and corruption.**
- **Respect** people of every tribe, religion and background.

## When rights are violated
You can seek help from the **Human Rights Commission**, the police, a lawyer or legal aid, or the courts. The next course, Making a Complaint, explains how.

## Know your rights calmly
Knowing your rights helps you speak up respectfully and confidently, for yourself and others.
key_points: The Bill of Rights protects every person
Rights come with responsibilities
The Human Rights Commission helps when rights are violated

lessons.title: Who to go to for what
lessons.body:
Many problems are solved faster when you go to the right office first. Here is a simple guide.

## Council
Markets, refuse collection, local roads and drainage, street lights, building plans, business levies and trading permits.

## Ministry district offices
- **Education:** schools, teachers, school places.
- **Health:** clinics, medicines, health workers.
- **Agriculture:** extension services and farmer support.
- **Community Development and Social Services:** social welfare and social cash transfer.

## Utilities and public bodies
- **ZESCO:** electricity faults, meters and tokens.
- **Your water utility:** water supply and bills.
- **ZICTA:** problems with networks, SIM registration and communications services.

## Documents
- **Department of National Registration, Passport and Citizenship:** NRCs, passports and citizenship.
- Birth and death registration: your district's registration office.

## Safety and justice
- **Police:** crime, accidents, threats. The **Victim Support Unit** helps victims of abuse.
- **Human Rights Commission:** violations of your rights.
- **Anti-Corruption Commission:** someone demands a bribe.

## Your representatives
Your **councillor** and **MP** can help when an office does not respond.

## Start local
Begin with the local office closest to the problem. If it is not solved, move up: the district head, then the provincial or national office, then an oversight body.
key_points: Start with the local office closest to the problem
Councils handle markets, refuse and local roads
Ask your councillor or MP if an office does not respond
lessons.try_it: Pick one problem in your area and decide which office should handle it.

lessons.title: How a law is made
lessons.body:
Laws affect everything from land to mobile money. Knowing how they are made helps you take part.

## The steps
1. **An idea.** A ministry, an MP or a commission sees a need for a new law or a change.
2. **Consultation.** Government often asks the public and organisations for views on draft laws. Watch for notices in newspapers, on the radio and on official pages.
3. **Publication.** The Bill is published in the **Government Gazette**.
4. **First reading** in the National Assembly, where the Bill is introduced.
5. **Committee stage.** A parliamentary committee studies the Bill and can invite **submissions** from the public and organisations.
6. **Second and third readings.** MPs debate and vote. They can change parts of the Bill.
7. **Assent.** The President signs it, and it becomes an **Act of Parliament**.

Changes to the Constitution follow a stricter process and need a larger majority in Parliament.

## How you can have a say
- Respond to public consultations.
- Make a **submission** to a parliamentary committee, alone or with a group.
- Talk to your MP about a Bill before the vote.
- Join or support community and civil society groups working on the issue.

## Reading laws
Acts are published by the National Assembly and on **ZambiaLII**, a free online library of Zambian law. Many organisations also publish simple summaries.
key_points: Bills pass through readings and committee before becoming Acts
The public can make submissions to committees
Read Acts free on ZambiaLII
